Paper_Info: Keystroke Dynamics: Concepts, Techniques, and Applications | RASHIK SHADMAN, AHMED ANU WAHAB, MICHAEL MANNO, MATTHEW LUKASZEWSKI, DAQING HOU, FARAZ HUSSAIN | 2025
Objective: Provides a detailed review of keystroke-based authentication systems and their applications, emphasizing their nonintrusive, cost-effective nature for cybersecurity.
Methodology: Comprehensive survey of recent developments in keystroke dynamics research (2013–present), categorized by contributions to datasets, algorithms, feature engineering, mobile device integration, and applications.
Dataset: Includes novel keystroke datasets, touch screen/mobile device data, and benchmarking resources. Covers free-text, fixed-text, and semi-fixed-text keystroke data.
Performance: Cost-effective, non-intrusive, and deployable remotely. Enables continuous authentication via free-text keystroke analysis.
Limitations: Focuses on existing datasets and algorithms; lacks coverage of emerging trends beyond 2022. Prior surveys concentrated on narrow aspects like mobile devices or specific algorithms.

Paper_Info: Identifying Users’ Emotional States through Keystroke Dynamics | Stefano Marrone, Carlo Sansone | NOT MENTIONED
Objective: Recognizing users’ emotional states using Keystroke Dynamics as a non-intrusive, cost-effective alternative to hardware-based emotion recognition methods.
Methodology: A time-windowing approach analyzes writing sessions in batches, using features derived from dwell time, flight time, and key press patterns to predict emotional states from short typing windows (e.g., 30 seconds).
Dataset: EmoSurv dataset with 124 subjects, containing keystroke data and emotion labels (Anger, Happiness, Calmness, Sadness, Neutral State) collected via fixed/free text typing tasks and emotion-inducing videos.
Performance: Short writing windows (30") achieved accuracy comparable to systems analyzing larger sessions (up to a few minutes) across metrics: Accuracy, F1-score, and AUC-ROC.
Limitations: Dataset size and diversity may limit generalizability; requires further validation on real-world scenarios.

Paper_Info: Estimation of the User’s Emotional State by Keystroke Dynamics | Rinky Solanki, Pragya Shukla | NOT MENTIONED
Objective: Traditional computer systems lack adaptability to user emotional states, necessitating methods to recognize emotions for intelligent HCI.
Methodology: Analyzes keystroke dynamics (timing and frequency parameters) to infer emotional states via fixed/free text input and user self-reports.
Dataset: Fixed text from 'Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland' and free text input with periodic keystroke monitoring.
Performance: Captures keystroke patterns and self-reported emotional states to train and compare models against database records.
Limitations: Relies on self-reported emotional states and may lack contextual awareness of complex emotional nuances

Paper_Info: AN IMPROVED MODEL FOR EMOTION-AWARE COMPUTING DEVICES USING KEYSTROKE DYNAMICS AND SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINE | ENYINNAH, CHIDIEBERE | NOT MENTIONED
Objective: Address limitations of existing emotion-sensing methods by proposing a model using keystroke dynamics and SVM to determine user emotions through typing patterns, avoiding expensive and invasive equipment.
Methodology: Keystroke dynamics analysis combined with SVM to create models for six emotional states. Field study collected keystroke data and self-reported emotional states for training.
Dataset: Participants' keystrokes and self-reported emotional states from a field study.
Performance: Cross-validation results to identify best-performing emotional state models. Validated models for six emotional states (Anger, Fear, Disgust, Happiness, Sadness, Surprise) with recommendations for future analysis.
Limitations: Emotions are fuzzy and context-dependent; cultural differences may affect emotional pattern generalization.

Paper_Info: NOT MENTIONED | Po-Ming Lee, Wei-Hsuan Tsui, Tzu-Chien Hsiao | 2014
Objective: Examine variance in typing patterns caused by emotional states
Methodology: Controlled experiment with IAPS-induced emotional states and two-way Valence × Arousal ANOVAs
Dataset: Keystroke data from 27 subjects under different emotional states induced by IAPS stimuli
Performance: Emotion significantly impacted keystroke metrics (p < .001), but individual variability dominated
Limitations: Emotional effect size is small compared to individual variability; previous methods may not fully capture variance sources
